description: Topic hierarchy for the ESSCE 2019 English paper (grammar-based; no textbook), linking grammar concepts, keywords, grammar references and exam questions.

topics.title: Reading comprehension
topics.concept: Answer only from the passage: find the sentence that the question paraphrases, check quantity words (all, most, only, never) and numbers, and choose ‘not stated’ when the text is silent.

subtopics.title: Stated details, true/false and ‘except’ questions
subtopics.concept: Scan for the key word, read the whole sentence, and match the paraphrase. Options with ‘only’, ‘certainly’ or changed numbers are usually traps. For NOT/EXCEPT questions, cross out every option the text supports.

subtopics.title: Main idea, title and text organisation
subtopics.concept: A title or main idea must cover the whole paragraph or passage – not a single example (too narrow) and not a general subject (too broad). In well-organised texts each paragraph introduces one idea.

subtopics.title: Inference and the writer’s view
subtopics.concept: Inference questions ask what the writer implies. Base the answer on explicit clues (e.g. ‘a worldwide issue’ → a worldwide solution), never on outside opinion.

topics.title: Vocabulary and word choice
topics.concept: Work out meaning from context and know common collocations, idioms and phrasal verbs.

subtopics.title: Vocabulary in context (synonyms)
subtopics.concept: Replace the word with each option inside the original sentence; the correct synonym keeps the meaning (possess = have, convey = express, depletion = reduction, exacerbate = make worse, burgeoning = growing).

subtopics.title: Word choice, collocations and idioms
subtopics.concept: Some words go together: form a boundary, charity school, be in difficulties. Learn them as chunks.

subtopics.title: Phrasal verbs
subtopics.concept: Verb + particle with a special meaning: go off (alarm rings), knock down, break into, run off with (steal and escape).

topics.title: Verb forms: tenses, conditionals, passive, modals
topics.concept: Choose the verb form from time signals, the tense of the surrounding verbs and the meaning (active/passive, real/unreal).

subtopics.title: Tenses in context
subtopics.concept: Narratives use the past simple for completed events and the past perfect for earlier events; ‘by + future time’ signals the future perfect; stative verbs (want, know) are not used in continuous forms; verbs joined by ‘and’ are parallel.

textbook_refs.topic: Present simple – agreement in relative clauses

subtopics.title: Conditional sentences
subtopics.concept: First: If + present, will + base (never ‘will’ in the if-clause). Second: If + past, would + base. Third: If + had + V3, would have + V3.

subtopics.title: Passive voice
subtopics.concept: be + past participle in the needed tense: is questioned, was being built, to be ventilated; after verbs of perception: hear/see + object + being + V3. Active ↔ passive keeps the tense.

textbook_refs.topic: Subject–verb agreement: one of + plural noun

subtopics.title: Modal verbs
subtopics.concept: had better + base = strong advice/warning (often with ‘or else’); must = obligation; needn’t = no obligation.

topics.title: Sentence grammar: articles, agreement, quantifiers, prepositions, linkers
topics.concept: Small words that decide correctness: articles, agreement, quantifiers, prepositions, linking words, degree words and punctuation.

subtopics.title: Articles (a/an/the/zero)
subtopics.concept: a/an: first mention of a singular countable noun, ‘a hundred’, ‘quite a …’; the: specific or already known (the house next door, the back windows); zero article: plurals/uncountables in general.

subtopics.title: Subject–verb agreement
subtopics.concept: Titles of books and plays are singular (Romeo and Juliet was written…); check the head noun, not nearby nouns.

textbook_refs.topic: Present simple – agreement in relative clauses
Subject–verb agreement: one of + plural noun

subtopics.title: Quantifiers
subtopics.concept: little/a little + uncountable; few/a few + plural countable. Without ‘a’ the meaning is negative (almost none).

textbook_refs.topic: Quantifiers: a few / a little / many / much
Question words – How much / How many

subtopics.title: Prepositions and dependent prepositions
subtopics.concept: quarrel with, protect from, between (two) / among (more than two), foremost among, difficult for someone to do, break into, knock down, run off with.

subtopics.title: Linking words: contrast and purpose
subtopics.concept: although + clause; in spite of / despite + noun (never ‘despite of’); lest + (should) = so that … not; so that + clause; so as to + infinitive.

textbook_refs.topic: Purpose clauses: so that / in order to

subtopics.title: Degree and comparison (too, so, very)
subtopics.concept: too + adjective = more than acceptable; so + adjective + that-clause; comparatives: higher than, larger than (never ‘more older’/‘very older’).

subtopics.title: Punctuation
subtopics.concept: Reported questions end with a full stop and use statement word order; direct questions have a question mark inside the quotation marks.

topics.title: Spoken-English structures: tags, additions, short answers
topics.concept: Short responses repeat the auxiliary of the first sentence and reverse or keep polarity according to the rule.

subtopics.title: Question tags
subtopics.concept: Positive statement → negative tag and vice versa; negative words (no one, never) count as negative; no one/everyone → they; Let’s … shall we?

subtopics.title: Additions (so/neither/nor/either)
subtopics.concept: Negative: Neither/Nor + auxiliary + subject, or subject + auxiliary + not, either. Positive: So + auxiliary + subject, or subject + auxiliary, too.

subtopics.title: Short answers – agreeing and disagreeing
subtopics.concept: Agree with a positive: Yes, it is. Agree with a negative: No, I haven’t. Use the same auxiliary as the statement.

subtopics.title: Conversation completion
subtopics.concept: Read the lines before AND after the gap: the reply (‘Yes, it is.’) tells you the form of the question; the next line tells you what the speaker is reacting to.

textbook_refs.topic: Functional language – asking for and giving directions
Question words – How much / How many

topics.title: Sentence meaning and transformation
topics.concept: Recognise sentences with the same meaning and transform direct ↔ indirect speech.

subtopics.title: Sentence meaning / paraphrase (idioms)
subtopics.concept: can’t help + -ing = can’t stop oneself; nothing short of X = only X; ‘only … however’ puts the weight on the second idea.

subtopics.title: Reported (indirect) speech
subtopics.concept: After a past reporting verb, backshift tenses; questions take statement order and a full stop; exclamations → exclaimed how/what … or exclaimed that it was very …. Undo all of this when changing back to direct speech.

subtopics.title: Inversion after negative/limiting adverbials
subtopics.concept: After Not only, Never, Seldom, Hardly, No sooner, Only then … at the start of a clause, use question word order: Not only does the bank provide …

subtopics.title: Active ↔ passive transformation
subtopics.concept: Keep the tense: past continuous active (was treating) ↔ past continuous passive (were being treated); the object becomes the subject and the verb agrees with it; questions keep question word order and the question mark.

subtopics.title: Connecting clauses correctly (although/despite/in addition to)
subtopics.concept: although/though + clause; despite/in spite of + noun or -ing; in addition to/besides + -ing for adding; because/since give reasons, so they cannot join contrasting ideas.

topics.title: Paragraph writing
topics.concept: A paragraph has one main idea: topic sentence, supporting sentences with examples and linkers, and a concluding sentence. It is marked on content, organization and language.

subtopics.title: Paragraph writing (argument / comparison–contrast)
subtopics.concept: Plan for 10 minutes, write about 200 words, then check for 5–10 minutes. Comparison paragraphs use whereas, while, on the other hand, both and comparatives. Effect paragraphs use first of all, secondly, as a result and finally.

textbook_refs.topic: Paragraph writing – topic sentence, supporting sentences, concluding sentence
Cause–effect paragraph (as a result, therefore, so) and descriptive/chronological paragraph (first, then, after that, finally)
Present simple for routines with adverbs of frequency
